claims.source: We also compared the effect of adding 5%, 10%, and 20% coconut oil in ND and found that the effect of HFD to enhance starvation-induced hyperactivity was dose-dependent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, which compares different concentrations of coconut oil.

claims.claim: HFD-fed flies exhibited significantly increased walking speed before locating food sources.
claims.source: We found that HFD-fed flies exhibited significantly increased walking speed and significantly decreased latency before locating and occupying the food sources (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C from video recording-based food seeking assay.

claims.claim: HFD-fed flies exhibited significantly decreased latency before locating and occupying food sources.
claims.source: We found that HFD-fed flies exhibited significantly increased walking speed and significantly decreased latency before locating and occupying the food sources (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C from video recording-based food seeking assay.

claims.claim: Total visits to food and the duration to stay on food remained unchanged in HFD-fed flies.
claims.source: whereas their total visits to food and the duration to stay on food remained unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D-E from video recording-based food seeking assay.

claims.claim: Coconut oil and lard, which were rich in saturated fat, significantly enhanced starvation-induced hyperactivity.
claims.source: Coconut oil and lard, which were rich in saturated fat (Segarra et al., 2002), significantly enhanced starvation-induced hyperactivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and cited literature on fat composition.

claims.claim: Soybean oil, which was mostly unsaturated fat, did not affect starvation-induced hyperactivity.
claims.source: In contrast, soybean oil, which was mostly unsaturated fat (Henkel et al., 2018), did not affect starvation-induced hyperactivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and cited literature on fat composition.

claims.claim: High-sugar diet (HSD) did not enhance starvation-induced hyperactivity.
claims.source: High-sugar diet (HSD) did not enhance starvation-induced hyperactivity, either (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: ND-fed and HFD-fed flies exhibited comparable feeding activity in the FLIC assay and the BARCODE assay.
claims.source: In contrast, ND-fed and HFD-fed flies exhibited comparable feeding activity in the FLIC assay (Ro et al., 2014) and the BARCODE assay (Park et al., 2018; Figure 1J and K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J and K using two different feeding assays, with citations to the methods.

claims.claim: Flies' body weight was not affected by HFD.
claims.source: However, flies' body weight was not affected by HFD, and their lipid storage was actually significantly elevated by HFD (Figure 1L and M)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L measuring body weight.

claims.claim: Lipid storage was significantly elevated by HFD.
claims.source: However, flies' body weight was not affected by HFD, and their lipid storage was actually significantly elevated by HFD (Figure 1L and M)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M measuring triglyceride storage.

claims.claim: The energy expenditure of flies was not affected by HFD.
claims.source: The energy expenditure of flies was not affected by HFD. Evidently, when fed ad libitum, the CO2 production of HFD-fed and ND-fed flies was comparable (Figure 1N).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1N measuring CO2 production as a proxy for energy expenditure.

claims.claim: Upon 24 hr starvation, the body weight and lipid storage of both ND-fed and HFD-fed flies decreased.
claims.source: Consistently, upon 24 hr starvation, the body weight and lipid storage of both ND-fed and HFD-fed flies decreased (Figure 1O and P)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1O and P measuring body weight and lipid storage after starvation.

claims.claim: Upon 24 hr starvation, the food consumption of ND-fed and HFD-fed flies increased in comparable manners.
claims.source: whereas the food consumption of these two groups of flies increased in the MAFE assay, in comparable manners (Figure 1Q, note that flies exhibited no food ingestion in the MAFE assay when fed ad libitum) (Qi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1Q using the MAFE assay, with citation to the method.

claims.claim: Five days of HFD feeding specifically enhances starvation-induced hyperactivity without altering flies' food intake and energy expenditure.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that five days of HFD feeding specifically enhances starvation-induced hyperactivity without altering flies' food intake and energy expenditure.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim based on multiple experimental results presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Starvation-induced hyperactivity of adult flies was driven by a specific group of OA neurons in the fly brain.
claims.source: We showed in a previous study that starvation-induced hyperactivity of adult flies was driven by a specific group of OA neurons in the fly brain (Yu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: The activity of OA+ neurons is regulated in opposite directions by two groups of functionally antagonizing hormones, the hunger-induced hormone AKH and the satiety hormones DILPs.
claims.source: As a hunger sensor, the activity of these OA+ neurons is regulated in opposite directions, by two groups of functionally antagonizing hormones, the hunger-induced hormone AKH and the satiety hormones DILPs.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous work, as indicated by the context.

claims.claim: ND-fed and HFD-fed flies showed comparable AKH and DILP2 mRNA production as revealed by both RNAseq and quantitative RT-PCR.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 2A–B, ND-fed and HFD-fed flies showed comparable AKH and DILP2 mRNA production as revealed by both RNAseq (Figure 2A) and quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B using two different methods.

claims.claim: Circulating AKH and DILP2 in flies' hemolymph were elevated and reduced upon starvation, respectively.
claims.source: Moreover, circulating AKH and DILP2 in flies' hemolymph were elevated and reduced upon starvation, respectively (Figure 2C–D)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D using dot blot analysis.

claims.claim: The levels of circulating AKH and DILP2 remained unaffected by HFD feeding under both fed and starved conditions.
claims.source: Nevertheless, their levels remained unaffected by HFD feeding under both fed and starved conditions, as shown by the dot blot using antibodies against AKH and DILP2 proteins (Figure 2C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D using dot blot analysis.

claims.claim: AKHR mRNA levels remained unchanged after HFD feeding, as revealed by RNAseq and quantitative RT-PCR.
claims.source: While AKHR mRNA levels remained unchanged after HFD feeding, as revealed by RNAseq and quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 2E–F)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-F using two different methods.

claims.claim: AKHR protein was significantly elevated in the head tissue of HFD-fed flies vs. that of ND-fed flies.
claims.source: AKHR protein was significantly elevated in the head tissue of HFD-fed flies vs. that of ND-fed flies, as demonstrated by western blot (Figure 2G–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-H using western blot analysis.

claims.claim: The production of dInR was not affected by HFD at both the transcriptional and translational levels.
claims.source: The production of dInR was not affected by HFD at both the transcriptional and translational levels (Figure 2E–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-H using multiple methods.

claims.claim: AKHR+ neurons in HFD-fed flies exhibited more robust calcium transients when stimulated with synthetic AKH than those in ND-fed flies in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: Indeed, by using a calcium imaging setup with ex vivo brain preparations, we found that these AKHR+ neurons in HFD-fed flies exhibited more robust calcium transients when stimulated with synthetic AKH than those in ND-fed flies in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2I–K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I-K using calcium imaging.

claims.claim: Blocking lysosome-mediated protein degradation by lysosome inhibitors chloroquine (CQ) and NH4Cl increased AKHR protein levels dramatically.
claims.source: To examine this possibility, we ectopically expressed HA-tagged AKHR protein in cultured Drosophila S2 cells, and found that blocking lysosome-mediated protein degradation by lysosome inhibitors chloroquine (CQ) and NH4Cl increased AKHR protein levels dramatically, while MG132 treatment to disturb proteasome function exerted little effect (Figure 3A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B using cultured cells and pharmacological inhibitors.

claims.claim: MG132 treatment to disturb proteasome function exerted little effect on AKHR protein levels.
claims.source: To examine this possibility, we ectopically expressed HA-tagged AKHR protein in cultured Drosophila S2 cells, and found that blocking lysosome-mediated protein degradation by lysosome inhibitors chloroquine (CQ) and NH4Cl increased AKHR protein levels dramatically, while MG132 treatment to disturb proteasome function exerted little effect (Figure 3A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B using cultured cells and pharmacological inhibitors.

claims.claim: AKHR may be mainly degraded via the lysosome pathway.
claims.source: Therefore, AKHR may be mainly degraded via the lysosome pathway.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing that lysosome inhibitors but not proteasome inhibitors affect AKHR levels.

claims.claim: Upon rapamycin treatment, HA-tagged AKHR protein was enriched in autophagosomes.
claims.source: Notably, upon rapamycin treatment, HA-tagged AKHR protein was also enriched in these autophagosomes (Figure 3C, red).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C using immunofluorescence imaging.

claims.claim: Inducing autophagy by both starvation and rapamycin resulted in significantly decreased AKHR protein levels in cultured S2 cells.
claims.source: Moreover, inducing autophagy by both starvation and rapamycin resulted in significantly decreased AKHR protein levels in cultured S2 cells (Figure 3D–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-E using cultured cells.

claims.claim: HFD suppressed autophagy in the AKHR+ neurons, as evident by the relative decrease of membrane-associated ATG8-II upon HFD feeding.
claims.source: Indeed, HFD suppressed autophagy in the AKHR+ neurons, as evident by the relative decrease of membrane-associated ATG8-II upon HFD feeding (GFP-ATG8-II/I, Figure 3F–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F-G using western blot analysis of ATG8 processing.

claims.claim: Specifically suppressing autophagy in AKHR+ neurons, by RNAi knock-down of two critical autophagy initiators ATG5 and ATG7, significantly enhanced AKHR accumulation in ND-fed flies.
claims.source: Additionally, specifically suppressing autophagy in AKHR+ neurons, by RNAi knock-down of two critical autophagy initiators ATG5 and ATG7, significantly enhanced AKHR accumulation in ND-fed flies (Figure 3H–I)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H-I using genetic manipulation.

claims.claim: RNAi knock-down of ATG5 and ATG7 in AKHR+ neurons both led to significantly enhanced calcium transients upon AKH administration in ND-fed flies.
claims.source: Indeed, RNAi knock-down of ATG5 and ATG7 in AKHR+ neurons both led to significantly enhanced calcium transients upon AKH administration in ND-fed flies (Figure 4A–B)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B using calcium imaging.

claims.claim: Blocking autophagy in AKHR+ neurons via RNAi knock-down of ATG5 significantly enhanced starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies without altering their baseline activity.
claims.source: Consistent with these results, blocking autophagy in AKHR+ neurons via RNAi knock-down of ATG5 significantly enhanced starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies without altering their baseline activity (Figure 4C–F)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-F using behavioral assays.

claims.claim: HFD feeding did not further enhance starvation-induced hyperactivity when autophagy was suppressed by ATG5/7 knockdown.
claims.source: In both conditions, HFD feeding did not further enhance starvation-induced hyperactivity (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4), likely due to the suppression of autophagy by ATG5/7 knockdown.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4, with inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: The head tissues of HFD-fed flies exhibited higher levels of p70S6K phosphorylation.
claims.source: Indeed, the head tissues of HFD-fed flies exhibited higher levels of p70S6K phosphorylation (Figure 5A–B), suggesting that HFD activated TOR signaling.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B using western blot analysis.

claims.claim: Upon HFD feeding, AMPK signaling (measured by the phosphorylation of AMPK) was suppressed.
claims.source: We found that upon HFD feeding, AMPK signaling (measured by the phosphorylation of AMPK) was suppressed, whereas AKT signaling (measured by the phosphorylation of AKT) remained unaffected (Figure 5C–D)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D using western blot analysis.

claims.claim: Upon HFD feeding, AKT signaling (measured by the phosphorylation of AKT) remained unaffected.
claims.source: We found that upon HFD feeding, AMPK signaling (measured by the phosphorylation of AMPK) was suppressed, whereas AKT signaling (measured by the phosphorylation of AKT) remained unaffected (Figure 5C–D)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D using western blot analysis.

claims.claim: Pharmacological activation of TOR signaling by MHY and suppression of AMPK by dorsomorphin both resulted in AKHR accumulation in cultured S2 cells.
claims.source: Indeed, pharmacological activation of TOR signaling by MHY and suppression of AMPK by dorsomorphin (dorso) both resulted in AKHR accumulation in cultured S2 cells, whereas suppression of TOR signaling by rapamycin and activation of AMPK by AICAR exerted the opposite effect (Figure 5E–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E-F using cultured cells and pharmacological agents.

claims.claim: Suppression of TOR signaling by rapamycin and activation of AMPK by AICAR exerted the opposite effect on AKHR accumulation.
claims.source: Indeed, pharmacological activation of TOR signaling by MHY and suppression of AMPK by dorsomorphin (dorso) both resulted in AKHR accumulation in cultured S2 cells, whereas suppression of TOR signaling by rapamycin and activation of AMPK by AICAR exerted the opposite effect (Figure 5E–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E-F using cultured cells and pharmacological agents.

claims.claim: Dorsomorphin and rapamycin feeding led to increased and decreased AKH sensitivity in AKHR+ neurons, respectively.
claims.source: Consistent with these in vitro results, dorso and rapamycin feeding led to increased and decreased AKH sensitivity in AKHR+ neurons, respectively (Figure 5G–H)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G-H using calcium imaging.

claims.claim: Suppressing TOR signaling in AKHR+ neurons by ectopic expression of dominant negative TORTED resulted in significantly decreased starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies.
claims.source: Indeed, suppressing TOR signaling in AKHR+ neurons by ectopic expression of dominant negative TORTED (Hennig and Neufeld, 2002) resulted in significantly decreased starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies, and these flies did not respond to HFD (Figure 6A–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-D using genetic manipulation, with citation to the method.

claims.claim: Flies expressing TORTED in AKHR+ neurons did not respond to HFD.
claims.source: Indeed, suppressing TOR signaling in AKHR+ neurons by ectopic expression of dominant negative TORTED (Hennig and Neufeld, 2002) resulted in significantly decreased starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies, and these flies did not respond to HFD (Figure 6A–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-D using genetic manipulation.

claims.claim: Rapamycin feeding suppressed starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies.
claims.source: Like TORTED expression in AKHR+ neurons, rapamycin feeding suppressed starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 using pharmacological treatment.

claims.claim: Rapamycin feeding enhanced the baseline locomotion of fed flies.
claims.source: Notably, unlike TORTED expression AKHR+ neurons, rapamycin feeding enhanced the baseline locomotion of fed flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that global suppression of TOR signaling may have a locomotor effect.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, with inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: RNAi knock-down of TSC1 in AKHR+ neurons resulted in upregulated starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies.
claims.source: Besides, we genetically activated TOR signaling in AKHR+ neurons, by RNAi knock-down of TSC1, a suppressor of TOR signaling (Wullschleger et al., 2006) and by the ectopic expression of a dominant negative form of AMPK (AMPKDN) (Wullschleger et al., 2006). Both manipulations resulted in upregulated starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies (Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 using genetic manipulation, with citation to the method.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of a dominant negative form of AMPK (AMPKDN) in AKHR+ neurons resulted in upregulated starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies.
claims.source: Besides, we genetically activated TOR signaling in AKHR+ neurons, by RNAi knock-down of TSC1, a suppressor of TOR signaling (Wullschleger et al., 2006) and by the ectopic expression of a dominant negative form of AMPK (AMPKDN) (Wullschleger et al., 2006). Both manipulations resulted in upregulated starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies (Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 using genetic manipulation, with citation to the method.

claims.claim: Only one of the three lipoproteins, named Lipid Transfer Particle (LTP), but not the other two [Lipophorin (LPP) and Microsomal Triglyceride Transfer Protein (MTP)], was significantly upregulated in HFD-fed flies vs. ND-fed flies.
claims.source: We performed proteomic analysis of circulating proteins in flies' hemolymph by mass spectrometry (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—source data 2) and found that only one of the three lipoproteins, named Lipid Transfer Particle (LTP), but not the other two [Lipophorin (LPP) and Microsomal Triglyceride Transfer Protein (MTP)], was significantly upregulated in HFD-fed flies vs. ND-fed flies (Figure 7A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B using mass spectrometry.

claims.claim: Both triglycerides and cholesterol were enriched in the hemolymph of HFD-fed flies.
claims.source: Meanwhile, both triglycerides and cholesterol were enriched in the hemolymph of HFD-fed flies (Figure 7C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C-D using biochemical assays.

claims.claim: Among seven identified lipophorin receptors in Drosophila, lipophorin receptor 1 (LpR1) was most abundantly expressed in AKHR+ neurons.
claims.source: To this aim, we carried out single cell RNAseq analysis for individual AKHR+ neurons harvested from the fly brains in situ. Among seven identified lipophorin receptors in Drosophila, lipophorin receptor 1 (LpR1) was most abundantly expressed in AKHR+ neurons (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E using single-cell RNAseq.

claims.claim: RNAi knock-down of LpR1 in AKHR+ neurons eliminated the effect of HFD on AKHR accumulation.
claims.source: We thus examined the potential role of LpR1 in mediating the effect of HFD feeding on AKHR accumulation and starvation-induced hyperactivity. RNAi knock-down of LpR1 in AKHR+ neurons eliminated the effect of HFD on AKHR accumulation (Figure 7F–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F-G using genetic manipulation.

claims.claim: Flies with LpR1 knockdown in AKHR+ neurons did not respond to HFD feeding with an enhancement of starvation-induced hyperactivity.
claims.source: Consistently, these flies did not respond to HFD feeding with an enhancement of starvation-induced hyperactivity (Figure 7H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H using behavioral assays.

claims.claim: Knocking down LpR1 in the fat body generated diet-independent hyperlipidemia in ND-fed flies.
claims.source: By knocking down LpR1 in the fat body, the major organ for lipid storage and metabolism (Zheng et al., 2016), we generated diet-independent hyperlipidemia in ND-fed flies (Figure 8A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A-B using genetic manipulation, with citation to the method.

claims.claim: Compared with the control group, the phosphorylation of p70S6K in the diet-independent hyperlipidemia group was significantly up-regulated.
claims.source: We then asked whether diet-independent hyperlipidemia had similar effects on AKHR accumulation and starvation-induced hyperactivity as HFD feeding. Compared with the control group, the phosphorylation of p70S6K in the diet-independent hyperlipidemia group was significantly up-regulated (Figure 8C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C-D using western blot analysis.

claims.claim: Diet-independent hyperlipidemia led to upregulated AKHR accumulation.
claims.source: In addition, diet-independent hyperlipidemia led to upregulated AKHR accumulation (Figure 8E–F), mimicking the effect of HFD feeding.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E-F using western blot analysis.

claims.claim: ND-fed, hyperlipidemic flies showed significantly stronger starvation-induced hyperactivity than the two control groups.
claims.source: Consistent with these results, these ND-fed, hyperlipidemic flies showed significantly stronger starvation-induced hyperactivity than the two control groups (Figure 8G), which was comparable to that of HFD-fed flies (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8G using behavioral assays.

claims.claim: Starvation-induced hyperactivity in the fruit fly is composed of two behavioral components: increased sensitivity to food cues, and enhanced exploratory locomotion.
claims.source: Conceptually, food-seeking behavior in the fruit fly is composed of two behavioral components, increased sensitivity to food cues, and enhanced exploratory locomotion, which altogether facilitates the localization and acquisition of desirable food sources (Root et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: AKH acts as a hunger signal to activate its cognate receptor AKHR expressed in the fat body and subsequently triggers lipid mobilization and energy allocation.
claims.source: As an insect counterpart of mammalian glucagon, AKH acts as a hunger signal to activate its cognate receptor AKHR expressed in the fat body and subsequently triggers lipid mobilization and energy allocation (Bharucha et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: OA+AKHR+ neurons are functionally analogous to mammalian NPY/AgRP neurons in the hypothalamus.
claims.source: In that sense, these OA+AKHR+ neurons are functionally analogous to mammalian NPY/AgRP neurons in the hypothalamus, which also senses organismal metabolic states and regulates specific food intake behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on functional similarities between the two neuronal populations.

claims.claim: HFD feeding in mammals increases the excitability of NPY/AgRP neurons, which contributes to the hypersensitivity to starvation and increased food consumption.
claims.source: Notably, HFD feeding in mammals also increases the excitability of NPY/AgRP neurons, which contributes to the hypersensitivity to starvation and increased food consumption (Vernia et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Fasting induces autophagy in NPY/AgRP neurons via fatty acid uptake and promotes AgRP expression, which in turn enhances food intake.
claims.source: For example, fasting induces autophagy in NPY/AgRP neurons via fatty acid uptake and promotes AgRP expression, which in turn enhances food intake (Kaushik et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Eliminating autophagy in NPY/AgRP neurons reduces food intake and hence body weight and fat deposits.
claims.source: In line with these results, eliminating autophagy in NPY/AgRP neurons reduces food intake and hence body weight and fat deposits (Kaushik et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Loss of autophagy in POMC neurons displays increased food intake and adiposity.
claims.source: Conversely, loss of autophagy in POMC neurons displays increased food intake and adiposity (Coupé et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: HFD suppresses autophagy in different peripheral tissue types such as liver, skeletal muscle, and the adipose tissue.
claims.source: Accumulating evidence suggests that HFD suppresses autophagy in different peripheral tissue types such as liver, skeletal muscle, and the adipose tissue (Feng et al., 2016; He et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: HFD suppresses autophagy in the hypothalamus.
claims.source: Similarly, HFD suppresses autophagy in the hypothalamus, whereas blocking hypothalamic autophagy, particularly in POMC neurons, exacerbates HFD induced obesity (Coupé et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Blocking hypothalamic autophagy, particularly in POMC neurons, exacerbates HFD induced obesity.
claims.source: Similarly, HFD suppresses autophagy in the hypothalamus, whereas blocking hypothalamic autophagy, particularly in POMC neurons, exacerbates HFD induced obesity (Coupé et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: TOR is a highly conserved serine-threonine kinase that controls numerous anabolic cellular processes.
claims.source: TOR, a highly conserved serine-threonine kinase, controls numerous anabolic cellular processes (Proud, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Manipulating AMPK-TOR signaling results in the dysfunction of NPY/AgRP neurons as well as POMC neurons, which leads to abnormal food consumption and adiposity.
claims.source: Similarly, rodent studies have shown that manipulating AMPK-TOR signaling results in the dysfunction of NPY/AgRP neurons as well as POMC neurons, which leads to abnormal food consumption and adiposity (Kong et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Chronic over-nutrition, especially excessive intake of dietary lipids, is one of the leading causes of obesity and obesity-associated metabolic disturbances.
claims.source: Chronic over-nutrition, especially excessive intake of dietary lipids, is one of the leading causes of these metabolic disturbances (Bray and Popkin, 1998; Hill et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: HFD imposes adverse effects on the physiology and metabolism of liver, skeletal muscle, the adipose tissue, and the nervous system.
claims.source: Accumulating evidence has shown that HFD imposes adverse effects on the physiology and metabolism of liver, skeletal muscle, the adipose tissue, and the nervous system (Dietrich et al., 2013; Gómez-Pérez et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2015; Shimobayashi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Neurons located in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, particularly neurons expressing Neuropeptide Y (NPY) and Agouti-Related Neuropeptide (AgRP) or those expressing Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), are important behavioral and metabolic regulators.
claims.source: In rodent models, neurons located in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, particularly neurons expressing Neuropeptide Y (NPY) and Agouti-Related Neuropeptide (AgRP) or those expressing Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), are important behavioral and metabolic regulators (Belgardt et al., 2009; Ollmann et al., 1997; Stanley and Leibowitz, 1984).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: NPY/AgRP neurons detect various neural and hormonal cues such as circulating glucose and fatty acids, leptin, and ghrelin, and modulate energy intake and expenditure accordingly.
claims.source: These neurons detect various neural and hormonal cues such as circulating glucose and fatty acids, leptin, and ghrelin, and modulate energy intake and expenditure accordingly (Belgardt et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Upon the reduction of the internal energy state, NPY/AgRP neurons are activated and exert a robust orexigenic effect.
claims.source: Upon the reduction of the internal energy state, NPY/AgRP neurons are activated and exert a robust orexigenic effect (Belgardt et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Genetic ablation of NPY/AgRP neurons in neonatal mice completely abolishes food consumption.
claims.source: Genetic ablation of NPY/AgRP neurons in neonatal mice completely abolishes food consumption whereas acute activation of these neurons significantly enhances food consumption (Aponte et al., 2011; Krashes et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Acute activation of NPY/AgRP neurons significantly enhances food consumption.
claims.source: Genetic ablation of NPY/AgRP neurons in neonatal mice completely abolishes food consumption whereas acute activation of these neurons significantly enhances food consumption (Aponte et al., 2011; Krashes et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: NPY/AgRP neurons antagonize the function of POMC neurons that plays a suppressive role on food consumption.
claims.source: NPY/AgRP neurons also antagonize the function of POMC neurons that plays a suppressive role on food consumption (Roseberry et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: HFD increases the intrinsic excitability of orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons.
claims.source: For example, HFD increases the intrinsic excitability of orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons (Vernia et al., 2016)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: HFD induces leptin resistance.
claims.source: induces leptin resistance (Mazor et al., 2018; Olofsson et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: HFD enhances inhibitory innervations of NPY/AgRP neurons with anorexigenic POMC neurons.
claims.source: and enhances their inhibitory innervations with anorexigenic POMC neurons (Newton et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Maternal HFD, alcohol consumption, and aging disrupt normal food intake via affecting the excitability and/or innervation of NPY/AgRP neurons.
claims.source: Interestingly, besides HFD, other metabolic challenges, including maternal HFD, alcohol consumption, as well as aging, also disrupt normal food intake via affecting the excitability and/or innervation of NPY/AgRP neurons (Cains et al., 2017; Füredi et al., 2018; Rivera et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: NPY/AgRP neurons play a role in food-seeking behavior.
claims.source: It has been reported that NPY/AgRP neurons also play a role in food-seeking behavior (Aponte et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Food seeking and food consumption are temporally and spatially separated and even reciprocally inhibited.

results.result: Starvation-induced hyperactivity is a conserved behavioral trait across different wild-type fly strains, though both the magnitude and timing of onset vary between strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are supported by data from Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing behavioral responses across multiple wild-type strains. The data demonstrate both the conservation of the behavior and strain-specific variation in magnitude and timing.

results.result: HFD feeding specifically enhances starvation-induced hyperactivity in a dose-dependent manner without affecting baseline activity or food-seeking parameters other than walking speed and latency to food.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C8 and C18 are supported by multiple behavioral assays (DAMS, video recording) showing enhanced hyperactivity upon starvation in HFD-fed flies with dose-dependent effects (C5), increased walking speed and decreased latency (C6-C7), but unchanged baseline activity (C4) and unchanged food visits/duration (C8). The summary claim C18 accurately reflects these findings.

results.result: The enhancement of starvation-induced hyperactivity is specific to saturated fats (coconut oil and lard) but not unsaturated fat (soybean oil) or high-sugar diet.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 are supported by data from Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5, showing that saturated fats enhance the behavior while unsaturated fat and high sugar do not. The claims appropriately cite literature support for fat composition characterization.

results.result: HFD feeding does not alter food consumption, body weight, or energy expenditure, but increases lipid storage; upon starvation, both ND and HFD-fed flies show comparable metabolic responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C17 are supported by multiple metabolic assays (FLIC, BARCODE, MAFE, body weight, triglyceride, CO2 production) showing that HFD specifically affects starvation-induced hyperactivity without altering feeding behavior or energy expenditure. The increased lipid storage (C14) is consistent with HFD intake.

results.result: HFD feeding does not affect the production or circulating levels of hunger hormone AKH or satiety hormone DILP2 under fed or starved conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23 are supported by RNAseq, qRT-PCR, and dot blot data (Figure 2A-D) showing comparable mRNA and protein levels of AKH and DILP2 between ND and HFD-fed flies. Multiple orthogonal methods strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: HFD feeding increases AKHR protein levels in fly heads without affecting AKHR mRNA or dInR expression, resulting in enhanced sensitivity of AKHR+ neurons to AKH stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by RNAseq, qRT-PCR, western blot, and calcium imaging data (Figure 2E-K). The post-transcriptional increase in AKHR protein (C25) without mRNA changes (C24) and enhanced calcium responses (C27) provide a mechanistic link between HFD and behavioral changes.

results.result: AKHR protein is degraded primarily via the lysosome-autophagy pathway rather than the proteasome, as demonstrated by pharmacological inhibition and autophagy induction experiments in cultured cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are supported by in vitro experiments (Figure 3A-E) using lysosome inhibitors (CQ, NH4Cl), proteasome inhibitor (MG132), and autophagy inducers (rapamycin, starvation). The enrichment of AKHR in autophagosomes (C31) and decreased levels upon autophagy induction (C32) support the lysosomal degradation pathway.

results.result: HFD suppresses autophagy in AKHR+ neurons, and genetic suppression of autophagy by ATG5/7 knockdown mimics the effect of HFD on AKHR accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by western blot analysis of ATG8 processing (Figure 3F-G) and genetic manipulation experiments (Figure 3H-I). The decreased ATG8-II/I ratio upon HFD (C33) and increased AKHR upon ATG5/7 knockdown (C34) establish the link between HFD, autophagy suppression, and AKHR accumulation.

results.result: Genetic suppression of autophagy in AKHR+ neurons by ATG5/7 knockdown enhances AKH sensitivity and starvation-induced hyperactivity in ND-fed flies, phenocopying HFD effects, and HFD does not further enhance hyperactivity in these flies.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 are supported by calcium imaging (Figure 4A-B) and behavioral assays (Figure 4C-F). The enhanced calcium responses (C35), increased hyperactivity (C36), and lack of additional HFD effect (C37) demonstrate that autophagy suppression is sufficient to mimic HFD effects.

results.result: HFD feeding activates TOR signaling (increased p70S6K phosphorylation) and suppresses AMPK signaling in fly heads, while AKT signaling remains unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by western blot analysis (Figure 5A-D) showing increased p70S6K phosphorylation, decreased AMPK phosphorylation, and unchanged AKT phosphorylation. These data establish the signaling pathway changes induced by HFD.

results.result: Pharmacological manipulation of AMPK-TOR signaling bidirectionally regulates AKHR accumulation in cultured cells and AKH sensitivity in AKHR+ neurons in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 are supported by in vitro experiments with pharmacological agents (Figure 5E-F) and in vivo calcium imaging (Figure 5G-H). The bidirectional effects of TOR activation/suppression and AMPK suppression/activation on AKHR levels and neuronal sensitivity establish AMPK-TOR signaling as a key regulator.

results.result: Genetic and pharmacological manipulation of TOR signaling in AKHR+ neurons bidirectionally regulates starvation-induced hyperactivity, with TOR suppression decreasing and TOR activation increasing the behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 are supported by behavioral assays using genetic manipulations (TORTED, TSC1 RNAi, AMPKDN) and pharmacological treatment (rapamycin) (Figure 6 and supplements). The bidirectional effects establish TOR signaling as necessary and sufficient for regulating starvation-induced hyperactivity. The caveat about rapamycin's effect on baseline locomotion (C47) is appropriately noted.

results.result: HFD feeding specifically upregulates the lipoprotein LTP (but not LPP or MTP) and increases circulating triglycerides and cholesterol in hemolymph; LpR1 is the most abundantly expressed lipophorin receptor in AKHR+ neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by mass spectrometry proteomics (Figure 7A-B), biochemical assays (Figure 7C-D), and single-cell RNAseq (Figure 7E). The specific upregulation of LTP and identification of LpR1 as the cognate receptor in AKHR+ neurons establish a potential mechanism for lipid sensing.

results.result: LpR1 knockdown in AKHR+ neurons eliminates the effect of HFD on AKHR accumulation and starvation-induced hyperactivity enhancement.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by western blot (Figure 7F-G) and behavioral data (Figure 7H), but the authors note confounding effects including slightly elevated baseline hyperactivity and increased baseline locomotion in LpR1 knockdown flies. These confounds make it difficult to definitively conclude whether LpR1 knockdown specifically blocks HFD effects or has broader behavioral effects.

results.result: Diet-independent hyperlipidemia generated by LpR1 knockdown in the fat body phenocopies HFD effects, activating TOR signaling, increasing AKHR accumulation, and enhancing starvation-induced hyperactivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by biochemical assays (Figure 8A-B), western blots (Figure 8C-F), and behavioral assays (Figure 8G). The ability of diet-independent hyperlipidemia to mimic HFD effects demonstrates that elevated circulating lipids are sufficient to induce the observed changes, supporting the proposed mechanism.

results.result: The authors establish the background that starvation-induced hyperactivity in Drosophila is regulated by OA+AKHR+ neurons that sense metabolic state via antagonistic hormones AKH and DILPs, analogous to mammalian NPY/AgRP neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20, C59-C61, C86-C87, C89-C90 are supported by citations to the authors' previous work and established literature. These claims provide essential context for the current study and are appropriately referenced.

results.result: The authors provide extensive background on mammalian NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons, HFD effects on hypothalamic function, autophagy regulation, AMPK-TOR signaling, and the conservation of metabolic regulation between flies and mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C85 and C88 are supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These background claims establish the broader context and relevance of the study, particularly the parallels between fly and mammalian systems.

results.result: The authors propose a mechanistic model where HFD-induced excess dietary lipids are transported by LTP to AKHR+ neurons via LpR1, suppressing autophagy-dependent AKHR degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 represent the authors' integrated model based on the collective experimental evidence presented in the manuscript. While individual components are well-supported, the complete mechanistic pathway from LTP-LpR1 signaling to autophagy suppression requires additional direct evidence. The model is reasonable given the data but represents an inference from multiple lines of evidence.
